page: Amazon Web Services m7i.4xlarge is a general-purpose instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features a custom Intel Xeon 8488C processor running at a base clock speed of 3.2 GHz on the x86_64 instruction set. The instance provisions 16 virtual CPUs across 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading, providing 48 KB of L1 data cache per core, 2 MB of L2 cache per core, and a shared 105 MB L3 cache pool. System memory is configured with 64 GB of DDR5 operating at 5 GHz, providing a standard general-purpose ratio of 4 GB of RAM per vCPU. No local storage is included with the instance, making external network storage necessary for persistent data handling. Network baseline bandwidth is provisioned at 6 Gbps, and no discrete GPUs are included in the configuration.

Benchmark evaluations position the m7i.4xlarge squarely in average performance bands for multi-core compute and general-purpose throughput, achieving a multi-core Geekbench score of 10710.0 and a multi-core stress-ng rating of 14645.49. Memory subsystems show strong large-block uncached read and write bandwidth at 75.78 GB/sec and 64.35 GB/sec, respectively. A notable operational highlight is its Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) and AVX-512 hardware support, which facilitates acceleration for specific arithmetic patterns; this is reflected in small-model text generation reaching 333.79 tokens per second, placing it within top-tier performance percentiles for lightweight model execution.

From an infrastructure efficiency perspective, the m7i.4xlarge provides a balanced hardware ratio suited for mixed resource demands without skewing toward heavy compute or memory premiums. The primary operational tradeoff stems from the absence of integrated local NVMe disks, which shifts all high-IOPS demands onto network-attached storage and network capacity constraints. The instance is technically well aligned with backend application servers, container clusters, relational databases, continuous integration build jobs, and caching services such as Redis, where balanced CPU and DDR5 memory density are the primary constraints.

It provides 16 dedicated virtual CPUs across 8 physical cores at 3.2 GHz, alongside a 105 MB L3 cache. Memory capacity is fixed at 64 GB of DDR5 operating at 5 GHz, delivering a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory allocation. There is no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached storage volumes, and baseline network throughput is rated at 6 Gbps. The processor features hardware support for Advanced Matrix Extensions and AVX-512, which assists low-parameter model execution, reaching 333.79 tokens per second in small-model text generation tests. The instance delivers stable memory bandwidth and multi-core CPU capacity, making it technically suitable for containerized microservices, relational databases, continuous integration pipelines, and general enterprise application hosting.
